speechtext:
The first purpose of this bill is to establish the office of a proctor to examine into parliamentary divorce proceedings. This is particularly essential because this house has passed a bill which eliminates all effective appeal procedures. If this bill were passed people would be able to appeal to the proctor, and I believe the other place is very interested in that.
Second, this bill would allow the Minister of Justice to refer appeals to the proctor rather than to his own department because, as he himself has said, constitutionally these appeals are probably not within his jurisdiction. Third, this bill would establish a joint committee of the two houses which would have the right to set up rates to be charged by the various people concerned with divorce petitions such as lawyers, parliamentary agents, detectives and others, with a view to lowering the cost of parliamentary divorce proceedings.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence and ask if he would make a report to the house on the circumstances surrounding the fire which destroyed the main building of the defence radar research laboratory in Prince Albert, and especially on the adequacy of fire protection equipment available to cope with this fire.

subtopic: PRINCE ALBERT, SASK.    DESTRUCTION BY FIRE OF RESEARCH LABORATORY

Mr. Speaker, I have a report here on the fire so far as it has been possible to secure one up to date. It is as follows.
The main building of the defence research board's Prince Albert radar laboratory was heavily damaged by fire in the early evening of January 31. The Prince Albert fire department was unable to extinguish the blaze, but was able to limit the damage to the transmitter area in the main building. The tower and antenna were not damaged. The major portion of the test equipment, receiving equipment and office furnishings were saved and removed to storage. A temporary office has been set up in the armoury at Prince Albert. No one was injured.
The Prince Albert radar laboratory is operated by the defence research telecommunications establishment, Ottawa. A senior officer of this organization and three other members of the staff are flying to Prince Albert this afternoon in order to carry on an official inquiry into the circumstances of the fire, which will be started immediately. The extent of the loss, of course, cannot be estimated at the present time, nor the length of time that the laboratory will be out of action.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES STATEMENT ON AIR CREW COMPLEMENT FOR NEW PLANES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES STATEMENT ON AIR CREW COMPLEMENT FOR NEW PLANES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Thursday the hon. member for Laurier inquired regarding the air crew complement on T.C.A.'s newer aircraft types. The number of air crew required on duty in the cockpit of a plane is subject to approval of the Department of Transport. It is determined in relation to such factors as aircraft handling characteristics, cockpit visibility, instrumentation and controls, general cockpit layout, and a number of other factors.
In the case of the DC-8, the department required that the cockpit complement be three persons. Two of these, of course, would be pilots, but it was left to T.C.A. to determine whether the third person should be a pilot or flight engineer. In fact I understand that T.C.A. is carrying a third pilot.
With regard to the newly acquired Vanguard aircraft, a thorough examination of the


requirements for flight crew has been completed. My technical officers have taken into consideration the representations made by the Canadian air line pilots' association, the views of the most experienced supervisory pilots of T.C.A. and reports from air carrier inspectors of the civil aviation branch of my department who have made in-flight investigations including all normal and emergency manoeuvres in the air.
As a result it has been concluded that this particular model of Vanguard aircraft, which has a cockpit especially designed to T.C.A. requirements, does not require three pilots, and that operational safety can be maintained with two on all routes on which T.C.A. intends operating the aircraft initially at least. Our examination of the problem, however, indicated that the qualifications for first officer or co-pilot established some years ago and requiring that a first officer hold a commercial pilot licence only did not visualize the introduction of aircraft of the size and performance of the Vanguard, and it has therefore been decided to require that first officers in Vanguard aircraft be technically trained to the standard of a fully qualified captain and that such first officers shall be required to hold a valid air line transport pilot licence. This increased requirement is designed to ensure that in the event of incapacitation of the captain, the aircraft will be in the charge of a person who is technically competent to act as captain in an emergency and will be in possession of the higher minimum experience requirements necessary to hold an air line transport pilot licence.

subsubtopic: EMPLOYMENT OF U.S. CITIZENS IN PIPE LINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 30 last the hon. member for Kootenay West directed a question to the Minister of Labour with respect to whether the minister had received any complaints concerning the numbers of United States citizens admitted to Canada for employment in the construction of pipe lines in British Columbia.
This is the time of year when such complaints begin to come in and we have received a number, particularly from the leader of the C.C.F. group in the house and house leader of the New party, the hon. member for Assiniboia. I can assure him that we are examining each and every complaint that is brought to our attention, and that officials of the national employment service have orders to make strict application of regulations regarding the admission of workers. No one is being approved by the national employment service to do any job for which a qualified Canadian is available.
We are receiving excellent co-operation in this regard from the department of my collegue the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. If the hon. member for Kootenay

West has any particular cases in mind in particular areas I would ask that he specify such cases, and I assure him that I will get a report in each case.

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE ON RADIO AND TELEVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday afternoon I started to reply to some of the matters which had been raised during this debate, and I had referred particularly to arguments advanced by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, who was the first speaker following the calling of the motion. I dealt with the point he raised as to the scope of the resolution and also the second matter with which he dealt and to which I replied at that time.
The hon. member also raised a question which he has brought up in every debate since I have been in this place, the argument that there should be a fixed parliamentary grant for the C.B.C. over a period of years rather than one vote by parliament each year. I have dealt with this matter on other occasions and I do not propose to spend much of the time of the committee this afternoon in repeating matters which I have stressed before. However, there are one or two obvious questions that arise in considering this matter. Over how long a period would such a fixed vote be scheduled? Would it be for one year, which is what we have now, or two, three or five years?
In theory an argument can be advanced for this procedure. If this nation had attained its full growth, if our territories were fully served by the C.B.C. or by private networks, if electronic devices had reached the climax of their development so there would not be revolutionary changes from year to year, if decisions had been made with respect to the institution of colour rather than black and white television; if all these matters were settled I think it would be fairly easy to 90205-6-103
Broadcasting
prognosticate the amount of money which should be allocated to the C.B.C. over a period of three, four or five years and vote it accordingly. But under the circumstances as they exist today, with the necessity of expanding our facilities in various areas in Canada, with the great electronic developments which are taking place and which render obsolescent equipment which the year before was thought to be adequate; with all the other questions with which the corporation has to deal, I suggest that this is not the time for us to fix an amount or even apply a formula of some kind applicable over a period of years.
How would one work out a formula? I have figures before me covering the years during which I have had some responsibility for the C.B.C. In the year 1957-58, the first year in which I had any responsibility, the corporation drew from the public treasury $41,600,000. The next year the amount was $51,900,000, an increase of $10,300,000. The next year there was an increase of only a little over $1 million, and the corporation drew down from the public treasury $52,300,000. The next year the amount was $60 million even, an increase of about $8 million. This year it is estimated the amount will be $70,418,000, an increase of about $10,400,000.
If one looks at commercial revenues, to which reference was made, one finds that in the year 1957-58 they amounted to $15,500,000;	1958-59,	$21,700,000;	1959-60,
$27,200,000. The next year there was an increase of only a few hundred thousand dollars and this year there will be a drop of about $300,000. Now, Mr. Speaker, one would need to have the wisdom of Solomon and the gift of prophecy of the late Joseph Howe, as well as a few other attributes that have not been given to mortal men, even in the Conservative government of this country, to make a reasonable prognostication or arrive at a formula upon which you could operate without putting the C.B.C. in a strait-jacket on the one hand or, from time to time, providing it with too much money. I say "too much money", but too much money is always a figure of speech so far as that corporation is concerned because there are many demands upon it, legitimate demands.
We remember when the taxation schedule was in effect and when the C.B.C. was in receipt of the excise tax on the sale of television sets. The sales of these sets were going up by leaps and bounds and there was a tremendous accretion to the treasury of the C.B.C., far more than its demands. When the demand for television sets levelled off the revenue of the C.B.C. fell off accordingly. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, therefore, that the

Broadcasting
proper procedure is the one which we are following at this time. I am not questioning for one moment the fact that the time may come when a change such as the one suggested by the Fowler commission should be made. It is easy to make these suggestions, but it is much more difficult to bring them into operation. I say at this time the policy of this government is to maintain the present system of parliamentary grants. This government is prepared to trust parliament. We believe in the supremacy of parliament, and that is the policy which is going to be followed in the immediate future.
What reason is there for suggesting a change? The only reason we have ever heard, Mr. Speaker, is the possibility of the corporation being under pressure from the government. The other day a suggestion was made that the corporation might be under pressure from the treasury board or it might be under executive pressure. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickers-gill) quite properly said that it was just as necessary to avoid executive pressure on the C.B.C. as it was necessary and advisable to make sure that the judiciary of this country is not under executive pressure. I could not agree more with that position.
During the time that I have been reporting for the C.B.C. I have never heard any suggestion of the corporation being under executive pressure in any way, shape or form. I have seen no letters from my friends of the C.C.F. party pointing out any incident or complaining about it or referring to it. I have seen no letters from the official opposition with respect to such a matter. I have received no letters from anyone in Canada, pointing to any incident or any alleged incident which could possibly give suspicion to the fact that the corporation was under executive pressure. As a matter of fact, if one judges from the correspondence one gets, if there is any pressure it is not the pressure of the executive on the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation but it might be the pressure of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation on the executive. I think if there is any pressure anywhere, judging from the mail which I receive-I realize, of course, that we who are in the spotlight of politics are undoubtedly sensitive to political criticism and we have an allergy to this criticism which is not given to citizens further removed, and perhaps very fortunately further removed-

May I ask the minister one question? Is he distinguishing between executive pressure in so far as finances are concerned or all executive pressure?

speechtext:
I am thinking of all kinds of executive pressure. As I was saying, judging from the mail which one receives, and that is perhaps one yardstick, there certainly has been an increasing abundance of it suggesting that there has been pressures on the executive by the corporation; that is not for me to comment upon. I have seen no evidence of it. As I have said, there is no evidence whatever. There has never been a thought of executive pressure on the C.B.C., and I am sure there never will be as long as this government is in power, or any other government, I would hope.
We are following this policy at the moment, and there will be no change in it in the immediate future. Certainly one would almost think, dealing at least with one phase, C.B.C.- Radio Canada, if there is any major pressure it is the political pressure that Radio Canada has exercised in certain ways in the area which it serves. There are abundant complaints with respect to that. It is not for me to measure them, but I do know that there has been a tremendously increasing volume during the four years in which I have had some responsibility for reporting to parliament for the C.B.C.
The hon. member also brought up the question of the commercial policy of the C.B.C. He regretted the increase in advertising. I must say that I can get very irritated at excessive advertising as well. I recall one program to which I wanted to listen and there was sufficient advertising, although well within the scope of the regulations laid down by the board of broadcast governors, to rather irritate me. I said to myself, I will never buy that product again under any circumstances. This was perhaps a human reaction to advertising in that form. Anyone using the C.B.C. naturally has to guard against any excessive commercialism because I am sure it will redound against the corporation using it. We try to safeguard that by regulation by the board of broadcast governors, and we judge by the experience of the C.B.C. itself which has looked after that matter for many years.
If one is worried about excessive commercialism he should read, as I do from time to time, letters from United States citizens who live just south of the Canadian border or from Canadians who have moved, for business reasons, to the United States and away from the C.B.C. If one reads these letters one finds these people never appreciated the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation until they got away from it. They never knew what commercialism meant; they never knew about the way in which the airways could be saturated by blatant commercialism until they were subjected to some programs far removed from

the C.B.C. I know that for one letter in this vein that I receive the corporation gets thousands which commend the corporation for their restraint. As the figures I read a while ago indicate, there has been a substantial volume of commercial programs on the C.B.C.
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is a very expensive corporation. It costs more to run the C.B.C. now than it ever cost in the old days to run the Canadian National Railways. It costs almost as much as it did to run Canada itself at one time. The people demand extensive and expensive services. Undoubtedly expenditures have risen, and I suspect they will continue to rise. A certain amount of commercial revenue, therefore, is not only advisable but necessary and is good business on the part of the C.B.C. management. My own opinion is that we have not reached the stage where we can say that commercialism on the C.B.C. is interfering with the primary responsibilities of the C.B.C., that is the dissemination of the type of program outlined at the inception of the corporation. I believe that the programs of this type are being maintained at the present time.
I think one could say this in general, that the corporation is working out a reasonable compromise between commercial necessities on the one hand and the maintenance of a broad national system on the other hand. I want to congratulate the corporation on doing that. These are the four points which were raised by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), I believe, and I have dealt with them.

I am not in a position to answer that question at the moment. I should be obliged to get advice from the C.B.C. with respect to it. I would suggest, with deference, that this is a question which should be explored in the committee and I presume it will be explored there. If the hon. member wants me to get him any information from the C.B.C. prior to that time I shall be glad to do so.
I might say this in passing, although I am not sure that it is in order. One perhaps should not discuss what one may have in mind with respect to legislation to deal with the French network. However, I think this is a fair comment to make. The C.B.C. today-and I am speaking now very roughtly-or Radio Canada covers about one third of the operations of the corporation. It serves the whole province of Quebec and part of New Brunswick and has now gone as far west as Manitoba. The number of directors, who were allocated on a regional basis, in my opinion do not give adequate representation on the board of directors to Radio Canada. One cannot, of course, and one should not by legislation designate directors from a certain group, a certain region, or a certain race. I have considered this matter and the committee may consider it. I have considered recommending to parliament this year the enlargement of the board of directors. Some amendments to the act will have to be brought forward. I think I am prepared to recommend that the number of directors be enlarged by a reasonable number so as to give additional representation on the board to Radio Canada and those on the French network.
The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) dealt at some length and very forcibly

with what he said was an infringement of free speech having regard to the fact that certain programs-and I think they were Canadian citizen programs or Canadian forum programs-were interfered with or were in some way controlled by the board of broadcast governors. This is a matter which I think can be dealt with much more effectively in the committee itself than by me at this time. The circumstances to which the hon. member refers are well known. There are rules for controversial programs, where the time is usually used as a forum. The understanding is that all sides should be represented in those discussions.
In the case of an individual program or an individual station, if all sides are not represented and one side fails to show up or something of that kind, the station management can go ahead with what they have, with the one side represented, provided that they undertake to give the other side an opportunity to be heard at some future time so that both sides of the issue can be presented. But when you have a program emanating from a station and then that program is taped and sent off the next day or the day after to a score or more stations across the country which are not under this responsibility, then the taped program presents only one side of the question. That is in general the problem with which the board of broadcast governors is confronted. It is that phase for which they have made regulations and it is that phase which they would like very much to have examined by the committee when the committee has an opportunity to meet.
The hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) dealt at some length with the international service and the fact that the C.B.C. is curtailing its shortwave broadcast to western Europe. Because of the fact that this matter was the subject of a starred question it was necessary for me to deal with it in part this afternoon. However, because the hon. member for Essex East stressed it to such a great extent, I want to deal with it again here for a moment or two.
As I have already said, it is true that the international service to western Europe has been curtailed in certain languages. This is not the first time that has happened. It was curtailed to a marked degree or a substantial degree anyway five years ago and it has been curtailed still further within the last few months.
As I pointed out, there are two economic reasons for this. The north country is developing. At one time it was served by radio by the armed forces and other facilities. Those facilities have been breaking down, they are obsolete and worn out, and it is necessary now

to service the whole north country with adequate radio coverage. In order to do that we are using some of the facilities at Sackville for beaming radio programs into the north country. Another point is that it is very desirable that we get our programs into that highly developing country.
Africa, is a country where there is not such an extensive knowledge of Canada, and our existing service to Africa is being extended substantially. It is, of course, being done on the advice of the Department of External Affairs, which has always worked in close co-operation with the C.B.C. in handling these shortwave programs.
We are maintaining our services to eastern Europe on our shortwave facilities. Throughout there has been some comment about jamming, and so on, and it is interesting to note that reports indicate a substantial decrease in this jamming during the last few months. In Poland there is apparently no jamming now. There have been programs exchanged between Russian and Canadian stations, largely on athletic events, and there is a move on foot now to broadcast programs which might be emanating from Russia.
The old concept of the shortwave service has to be changed in this modern age, and I am told by the officials of the C.B.C. that because of tape recording and modern techniques a better program service will be available now to western Europe.
The hon. member spoke about losing trade because we did not have a shortwave service here. I am sure that if our exporters had to depend entirely on the C.B.C. for the development of trade they would not feel like paying taxes to maintain it on that ground alone.
In western Europe we have common ideas. We have an exchange of ideas and people back and forth at all times. Movement is free and their facilities are available to us for our recordings, programs, and so on. I am told we can give a better Canadian service by using these new facilities than we were ever able to give in the past by the conventional shortwave service which has been used for so many years.
There is a wealth of information, of course, which is available by recording, radio, television, and so forth. In that connection I have a memo here which I think sets forth this point very authoritatively. I am not going to bore the house with the figures of how many people have been served, and so on. There is always some question about this, but in fact there is a very substantial listening audience in eastern Europe for Canadian programs. It is because of this information which we have received that we are maintaining shortwave service to eastern Europe.
Broadcasting
I am told that as a result of the better reception made possible by local rebroadcasts of Canadian programs it is expected that the actual number of listeners in the countries concerned will remain substantially the same and might even increase. Thus the decision to eliminate shortwave broadcasts to these five countries would not appear to affect Canadian interests and influence there adversely. Indeed, improvements may occur and considerable savings in public funds will have resulted.
The memo goes on to say:
I should perhaps mention at this point that the Voice of America, the United States counterpart of the C.B.C.-I.S., does not broadcast by shortwave to the five countries in their national languages.
That is a memo which, frankly, I received from the Department of External Affairs on their reaction to this situation.
The hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), with his usual interesting, forceful manner, covered various facets of the C.B.C.'s operations. I do not intend to deal with all his points. I think I have already dealt with some of them. He raised a very interesting point, of course, and it was something which was raised impliedly by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate in referring to the advertising of United States publications: Just how far does a Canadian national organization go, which is created for the purpose of developing a Canadian culture and an essential Canadianism? Just how far does it go in emphasizing United States' institutions in broadcasts and telecasts? The hon. member pointed out-as was very obvious at that particular time-the telecast which had been made on the occasion of the inauguration of President Kennedy and repeated, I believe, over national systems here. He wondered what contribution that would make to the development of Canadianism and whether Canadian political figures would receive the same treatment in the United States.
It is a very interesting question. One sometimes wonders what treatment Canadian political figures do receive. I received a letter a while ago from Quebec complaining of the fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) did not appear on Radio Canada news the night of his Christmas telecast. I made inquiries respecting that matter and was informed that the Prime Minister was a political figure, and since his telecast had appeared at noon it was not thought proper that he should appear again that night, on the news, and Mr. Pearson's Christmas message was carried instead. It is to be noted that the President of the United States appeared three times on the occasion of giving his address on the state of the union. So there is a very interesting field there about which no one has the answer.

Perhaps I could have two or three more minutes in order to complete my remarks. There has been a pattern established in this country whereby radio and television licences have been granted in the past to interests which also control newspapers and one can hardly change that policy in midstream because if we were to do that I can imagine many newspapers in this country which would have to divorce themselves from radio and television. I think, sometimes, it would be a very good thing for this government if there had been no applications from newspapers, because then there would have been no resentment or criticism by those newspapers who have applied for television stations but failed to get them and who therefore felt that this government was, perhaps, more subject to criticism than would otherwise have been the case. In any event we have this system in Canada today as a result of which, according to the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), the people of Toronto will have available two television stations, the C.B.C. station manned by so many personnel of the Toronto Star that he wonders how that newspaper is ever produced; and if the hon. member expects the other television station to be manned by personnel of the Telegram there will be a great opportunity for a newspaper to do very well in Toronto.
The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) raised a question about service. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) raised various questions with which, I think, I have dealt in part. He also stressed the necessity of extending television in French speaking areas of Saskatchewan. As I have

said, I hope and believe that this will be done.
I agree entirely with the hon. member that it should be done.
The hon. member for Okanagan-Boundary (Mr. Pugh) brought up the question of low power relays. Similar questions asking for additional services were raised in respect of Grand Falls, Humber-St. George's, Halifax, and other areas, and in addition there were other hon. members who did not raise the question in the house but who wrote me notes and reminded me that they had been after me many times before in this connection. They hoped they would not be overlooked because they had not taken up the time of the house on this occasion. Among them was the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort (Mr. Rapp) who has written to me with particular reference to Tisdale.
Then, of course, there was the perennial question raised by the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Simpson) and the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Forbes) with respect to the extension of radio and television to northern Manitoba. This is a problem with which he has confronted me ever since I took up my present position. It is a very difficult problem. The government of Manitoba is servicing that country with a telephone system. It is going to cost a lot of money to extend television and broadcasting services to the north country. It will have to be done, and I am hoping some way can be worked out whereby with some co-operation we can reduce the cost of those services, because after all the C.B.C. has got to work within certain limits. If it costs, say, $50 per family to provide a service in one area while in another area, equally remote, a service can be provided for $15, hon. members can see the type of problem the C.B.C. is facing in this connection. We have discussed this question time and time again and I am hopeful, and quite confident, that some solution can be worked out.
I think I have covered, though inadequately and hastily, the points raised during the two days when this matter has been before the house. I appreciate the manner in which hon. members have brought these matters to my attention and I hope the committee will have a fruitful session. It will have several months of work before it. Even if we can get out of here by May 1, which we are all hoping to do, it will have three months in which to operate, and I am sure it will be able to make a report which will prove very helpful.

(a)	in the case of goods other than goods custom-made to specifications, goods of approximately the same class or kind are made or produced in Canada; and
(b)	in the case of goods custom-made to specifications adequate facilities exist in Canada for the economic production of such goods within a reasonable period of time.

(a)	the normal Canadian consumption of the goods described in subsection (2), and

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The resolution now before the committee contemplates certain amendments to the Customs Tariff. The text of the proposed amendments is actually contained in the resolution itself. This follows the practice of the house in giving to hon. members in precise legislative form the text of amendments to such statutes as the Customs Tariff and the Excise Tax Act. The practice, of course, with respect to amendments to the Income Tax Act is somewhat different. There it is the practice to state the gist or effect of certain amendments. But in the case of statutes such as those I have mentioned the practice is to set forth in the resolution the precise terms of the proposed amendments. That is true in the case before us.
The proposed amendment is to be found in Hansard of December 20 at page 1017. In the budget speech on that date I dealt at some length with the situation out of which the proposed amendment has arisen and the proposed effect of the change in legislation. I do not wish to cover again the ground I sought to traverse in my remarks that night. They are to be found at pages 1013 and 1014 of Hansard of December 20. Perhaps in this part of my opening remarks I might just touch briefly on some of the features of the proposed amendment.
The anti-dumping provisions of our customs laws date from the year 1904. They were introduced by the late Mr. Fielding. It was in the year 1907 that legislation was first introduced which makes use of the expressions "class or kind made in Canada" or "class or kind not made in Canada" or similar phrases embodying the class or kind principle. This again was a measure introduced by Mr. Fielding.
I have already said in general terms that originally this legislation embodying the class or kind concept was intended to be given a broad interpretation, and it was in fact given a broad interpretation until about a decade ago. I think it is an incontestable fact that the intention was that the reduction given off the ordinary rates of customs duty in the case of a class or kind of goods not made or produced in Canada was intended to apply to goods not directly competitive with those in Canada.
[Mr. Nowlan.l
As I have said that was the kind of interpretation that was always given to these phrases in the law until about the year 1950. In the earlier period the differences in the rates applicable on the one hand to goods of a class or kind made or produced in Canada and on the other hand of a class or kind not made or produced in Canada was not as great as latterly, but in these more recent times with a growing difference in these rates the incentive has been very greatly multiplied on the part of importers or on the part of producers in other countries who wish to export into the Canadian market to bring their goods within the definition of those of a class or kind not made in Canada.
In other words, the incentive in this regard has grown considerably. This has had the effect of increasing the litigation which has marked the period of the last decade. Indeed one can say that in the period up to the last decade the administration of the terms to which I referred was fair and workable but in the decades since-I am speaking now particularly of the 1950's-the litigation has greatly expanded. Indeed there has been what might fairly be called a welter of litigation. This is attributable to several factors, one of which I have mentioned, namely the fact that the incentives are very much larger now with a considerable widening of the difference in the rates applicable as between the two types, and on the other hand the fact that there has been a growing volume of imports. This has also had the effect of increasing the volume of litigation.
Another factor of considerable importance is that a trend developed which I think it not unfair to say gathered a fair amount of momentum in the course of all the litigation, a trend of departing from the original interpretation. The result of this has been an erosion of the original interpretation given to these expressions in the Customs Tariff and accompanying that erosion a lessening of the benefits enjoyed by Canadian producers from the Customs Tariff, a measure of protection of their competitive position that parliament certainly intended to give them and which they enjoyed under the recognized interpretations down to the period of the last decade.
I have already said something on the subject of the relationship of GATT to this question. The committee is aware that a number of the rates on various commodities which are affected by this phrase are bound under GATT, but the definitions contained in the present statute and order in council are not bound. They were not the subject of negotiation. The effect of the trend of interpretation of the definitions in the Customs Tariff in the past decade has been to give a windfall benefit to the producers of other countries

who are seeking markets in Canada, something that was not expected on the part of the negotiators who represented their countries in the various GATT negotiations, beginning with 1947.
Nowadays-and of course GATT has continuously emphasized this fact-when countries are in a position to reduce their tariffs they seek compensating trading advantages in the markets of other countries, particularly of countries which are interested in obtaining a reduction of the tariffs of the first country. These become very important in the course of negotiations when it becomes a matter of making exchanges of trading advantages.
The result of this course of decision in Canada over the past decade relating to words used in our own Customs Tariff has been to give to the exporters of other countries an advantage in our market for which there has been no corresponding concession made by those countries in their markets in favour of the exports of Canadian goods into those markets. That is why I refer to this as a windfall. It was something that was not to be expected on their part when the GATT agreements were first negotiated or in the early renewals. It was not paid for and it was not a matter of agreement at all. It has been a windfall benefit.
We do not think that under modern conditions a windfall benefit should be given to other countries unless Canada obtains corresponding benefits in their markets in the course of negotiations under the auspices of GATT. That has been the approach to this question in recent years and it is a sound approach.
The number of times these important phrases appear in the Customs Tariff is quite extraordinary. If you comb through the provisions of the Customs Tariff in detail you will find that the expression "of a class or kind not made in Canada" appears in 70 items and you have similar appearances of corresponding expressions such as "of a kind not produced in Canada", "of a class or kind not produced in Canada", "of a class or kind not manufactured in Canada", and so on. There are half a dozen other similar expressions appearing. There are many items in the Customs Tariff in which this expression or one similar to it appears.
What of the meaning of these words? I think it is common ground that in legislating with reference to business transactions it is desirable that the legislation be clear, that those who are entering into important business transactions under the provisions of the law should know what will be the consequences, particularly in relation to financial 90205-6-104
Customs Tariff
results. There have been definitions in the present section 6 of the Customs Tariff. They are subsections 9 and 10 of section 6. The present amendment would propose to repeal these two clauses, substitute new clauses and introduce certain new provisions. The new provisions are set forth in the resolution.
The effect will be to set up two types of goods under the broad category that we are discussing. They are goods that are made up according to specifications, which may be called custom made, and then there is the broad class of goods not of the custom-made type. In the amendment proposed we have two classes of goods, one described as goods "custom made to specifications" and the other described as "other than goods custom made to specifications", etc.
Definitions are provided in the amendment which it is believed will be of very great assistance in clarifying the law. In that way they will be of assistance to those who are entering into business transactions involving imports. These amendments will also have the desirable effect of restoring to the interpretation and administration of these provisions what was fully accepted until a decade ago when this process that I have described as one of erosion set in. In other words, we are proposing to restore to this concept the well recognized and established meaning that this concept and these phrases bore from 1907 right down to the beginning of the last decade.
In relation to this matter of definition there is an important point. I will enlarge on it in dealing with the proposed definitions as applied to the two classes of goods referred to in the new amendment. The statute, in the clauses to which I have referred, authorized the governor in council to establish the percentage of the normal Canadian consumption and to fix such percentage in defining whether goods are or are not of a class or kind made in Canada, and it was by an order in council that these powers were exercised. The order in council is P.C. 1618 of July 2, 1936. It provides that "articles shall not be deemed to be of a class or kind made or produced in Canada unless a quantity sufficient to supply 10 per centum of the normal Canadian consumption of such article is so made or produced".
In other words, there has never been a statutory provision defining the percentage of consumption in the Canadian market that must be produced in Canada before the article in question shall be deemed to be of a class or kind made in Canada. That has been a definition established by order in council in existence now for some 25 years and passed under the authority of the statute. One of the results of the amendment now submitted to the house is that this definition will no longer

Customs Tariff
rest upon an order in council. We are proposing that the house should legislate completely on this subject without the necessity of any recourse to the fixing of percentages by order in council.
With respect, I invite the committee to approach this question from the point of view of dealing with the amendments according to their terms and, I think, the clear sort of definition that is proposed in the amendments. There is no occasion whatever for exaggerated statements in relation to the purpose of this amendment. Since the resolution was introduced into the house on the evening of December 20 there have been statements describing it as a measure of high protectionism. It is nothing of the kind. The effect of this measure is to restore the concept that was accepted and, indeed, not challenged in this country up till a decade ago, a well established and unchallenged concept. The fact is that there has been an erosion of that concept since and that producers in other countries have taken advantage of that erosion and have been shipping into the Canadian market more than they would otherwise have been entitled to at these very low rates applicable in the case of goods of a class or kind not produced in Canada, and they have done so without Canadians obtaining any compensating advantage in the markets of other countries.
This is the point, and it is the essential point that the government has in mind in bringing this legislation before the house. There is no justification or warrant whatever for describing this, as it has been described in certain newspapers, as a measure of high protectionism. It is nothing of the kind.
If it will be of assistance to the committee I should like to draw attention now to what I believe to be the essential features of the amendment now proposed. Let me just recapitulate them briefly in the hope that it may be of assistance to the committee in the discussion to follow.
First, for the first time the legislation will contain a positive definition instead of merely a negative limitation. Thus the negative formulation that "goods shall not be deemed to be of a class or kind made or produced in Canada unless" would be replaced in respect of the entire subsection by the positive formulation that "goods shall be deemed to be of a class or kind made or produced in Canada if".
Since a positive definition is being introduced it is appropriate that it be placed in conjunction with all other definitions in the Customs Tariff, that is to say, immediately after section 2, and that is why it is proposed to insert now a new section numbered 2A. The positive formulation may be expected to 
eliminate the uncertainties which might have surrounded a mere limitation although in fact, in the past, words with a limiting effect have in general been applied by the department and the courts as if they were a definition.
Second. I have already drawn attention to the two kinds of goods, goods that are custom-made according to specifications and goods that are not custom-made according to specifications. Perhaps this latter group could be called, for simplicity's sake, "shelf goods". They are goods of a kind that may often be found upon shelves, in inventories or in stock.
Now, I have pointed out the difference that is drawn in the proposed amendment between these two types of goods. I point out that in regard to shelf goods we have a provision to be found in 2A (1) (a):
in the case of goods other than goods custom-made to specifications, goods of approximately the same class or kind are made or produced in Canada;
That is the definition or interpretation to be given to the words "of a class or kind made or produced in Canada". Then, in clause (2) of the amendment we have these words:
Notwithstanding subsection (1), goods other than goods custom-made to specifications shall be deemed not to be of a class or kind made or produced in Canada unless at least 10 per cent of the normal Canadian consumption of goods of the same or approximately the same class or kind are made or produced in Canada.
Now, Mr. Chairman, this is the second observation I wish to make in regard to shelf goods. The word "approximately" is now inserted. This is designed to restore the breadth and flexibility of the whole concept which has been gradually narrowed down by the decisions of the tariff board, supported by the courts, reversing the rulings of the department, departmental rulings that were in accord with the interpretation well established up until a decade ago. It should be noted that in many cases these departmental rulings were in effect, as I have indicated, at the time the tariff items involved in "class or kind" were bound by GATT.

May I clarify one point before the minister leaves it? When he says the interpretation was well established up to a decade ago, do I understand him to suggest that the tariff board and the courts changed their decisions or that appeals were taken to these bodies and their decisions differed from the interpretations of the departmental authorities?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes; I think if the hon. member will examine the record of what I have just been saying he will see that the changes have been brought about in the

narrowing of the concept, what I have described as a process of erosion that has oc-cured as a result of the decisions of the tariff board on appeals and decisions of the courts.
The third observation, Mr. Chairman, is on the 10 per cent requirement which also relates to shelf goods. This requirement has been transferred from the present order in council to the basic legislation and, at the same time, it is provided that "Canadian consumption" is to be "as determined by the minister". This change is designed to reduce uncertainty and eliminate profitless litigation.
In so far as this matter of the jurisdiction conferred upon the minister is concerned, there has been a good deal of misunderstanding in some of the newspaper articles that I have seen on this subject. It has been pretended that this clause is designed to destroy the jurisdiction of the tariff board and to vest in the Minister of National Revenue arbitrary powers. That is a far-fetched, indeed fantastic, misinterpretation of the language of the proposed amendment.
That is what it says.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not what it says. It is quite evident the hon. member for Trinity either has not read the clause or has not read it with any degree of adult understanding.
That is what it says in English. I do not know in what language you are reading it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Evidently the hon. member does not know how to read English.
Certainly you don't know how to read it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should like now to refer to the fact that the regular appeal procedure of the tariff board will remain open to those concerned with regard to (a) whether or not imported goods are of approximately the same class or kind as goods made in Canada; (b) the determination of the amount of Canadian production and (c) whether or not the number of articles manufactured in Canada does, in fact, constitute a minimum of 10 per cent of the normal Canadian production.
And that is not arbitrary power?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this illustrates how completely befuddled the hon. member for Trinity is. I am talking about the jurisdiction of the tariff board and the hon. member, lost in his usual fog, is talking about the arbitrary powers of the minister. I am not talking about the powers of the minister 90205-6-104J
Customs Tariff
at all, I am talking about the right of appeal to the tariff board, where the door is open. Perhaps the hon. member, until he comes out of his fog, had better remain silent.

The minister had better
address his remarks to the bill. It is a very important bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is an important one, which can be better understood without these gratuitous interruptions by the hon. member for Trinity who has not read the bill.

These interruptions are
brought about by your gratuitous references on the basis of personality.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will the hon. member for Ottawa West address his efforts to restraining his colleague from making these gratuitous and irrelevant interruptions?
No, he is trying to keep the minister in order.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The minister does not need this gratuitous assistance from the member for Ottawa West.
He could do with a model of some sort.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
He will not be looking to the hon. member for Ottawa West for any helpful instructions. He will take them from other sources, but not from the hon. member for Ottawa West who has been holding forth in his sepulchral tones.
Now, the fourth observation I should like to make on this subject in the hope that it will be of assistance to the committee is this: For the first time an attempt is made to grapple with the problem of "custom-made goods". There has been a good deal of discussion over the years, Mr. Chairman, in regard to this matter, and I think it is quite clear that it never was intended by any government that introduced words of this kind that custom-made goods should automatically be ruled as not made in Canada. However, the rulings of the courts have tended in that direction.
In the field of custom-made goods, each product is either unique or virtually unique. Accordingly, it has been found necessary, in the provisions relating to this field, to confer upon the Minister of National Revenue a discretion that is broader than was necessary with respect to mass-produced or "shelf" goods. This is the reason, and a very complete reason, in my mind, for the proposed provision with respect to custom-made goods put forward here. We have in the proposed amendment the following provision:
For the purposes of this act, goods shall be deemed to be of a class or kind made or produced in Canada if-

Customs Tariff
I shall now refer to clause (b):
-in the case of goods custom-made to specifications, adequate facilities exist in Canada for the economic production of such goods within a reasonable period of time.
This definition with respect to goods custom-made according to specifications will undoubtedly bring the position much closer to the original intention, to the established understanding and meaning of this legislation of a decade ago and will stop the process of erosion that has occurred in this period.
What does the minister mean by "a reasonable period of time"?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is a matter of fair interpretation. It will depend upon the nature of the particular goods. Naturally every one of these cases will have to be examined on its own circumstances, and regard will have to be had for all the circumstances such as the length of time it takes to bring a particular article into production. It is a matter in which regard will have to be had for the business practice in this situation and I think the hon. member will appreciate what may be regarded as a reasonable time will vary from one type of goods to another. Something might depend also in such situations on the extent to which order books were filled up.
Will the minister accept another question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

This thought just runs in my mind. Would you be obliged to have a firm offer from a producer in Canada to produce that type of goods; I refer to a firm offer from a producer in Canada indicating that he is going to produce the item or could produce it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. It is not necessary that it be a firm offer. However, in any situation that arises calling for an interpretation in this matter, regard obviously will be had for all of the circumstances that concern it. That does not necessitate a firm offer in the sense of a binding legal obligation. But when the question arises for determination with respect to one of these custom-made goods, it will be the duty of those who are given that responsibility under the legislation to determine whether, having regard to all the circumstances, adequate facilities exist in Canada for economic production of that item of goods within a reasonable period of time.
Will the minister permit a question, for the purpose of clarification?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes.
[Mr. Fleming (Eglinton) .1
Will the minister explain how you could make any determination of whether there was any demand for custom-made goods before you had a customer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I take it that we are still speaking of custom-made goods?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not shelf goods?
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
All right. With regard to custom-made goods, suppose the situation arises in respect of a Canadian importer or, let us say, of a manufacturer in another country who wishes to know what will be the tariff rate applicable to his goods if they are here in Canada. A ruling is asked for. It may be asked for in advance of actual entry. If entry occurs, of course, a decision must be made as of that time. That decision is important because the results can be substantial having regard to the wide difference in the applicable tariff rates. Regard will be had to capacity and that will involve a determination in Canada as to whether the facilities exist. It does not mean that goods of precisely the same type and manufactured according to precisely the same specifications must have been made previously. There are numerous situations in which goods that are similar in nature have been produced but not of precisely the same kind as those that are specified in the particular case. It is in this area that some rigid and hard decisions have been made in the past.
I am prepared to contend that it never was the intention of parliament and never was the intention of governments that introduced legislation of this kind down through the years since 1907 that where the capacity exists, it should be a precise requirement of the legislation that the particular item of goods should actually have been made before it shall be deemed to have been of a class or kind made in Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I must inform the committee that the minister's time has expired. I understand there is unanimous consent that he continue.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think I have completed my general remarks on the introduction of the bill. I realize there will be many questions. It is for the committee to decide whether they wish to ask questions now or later. I am here to serve the committee.

I was simply trying to elucidate the last point made by the minister. I think perhaps I did not make my

question sufficiently specific. However, taking the answer the minister gave, I understand that if an importer of some article that is not now an article that is made currently in Canada-that is, a custom-made article- goes to the department and asks for a ruling the department would then have an onus put on it to search around Canada in order to find out whether there was capacity to make this article before giving an answer as to what the duty was. However, a great many people order things, although perhaps not a custom-made article of the kind the minister has in mind, and they do not go and ask the department for a ruling in advance. Indeed, I am not sure whether the department would give it. What I should like to know is what the modus operandi is here? I think we should all like to know this because we cannot form any judgment about this matter without knowing it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think there is one circumstance bearing on this question that will help to answer the question of the hon. member. What we are dealing with here are, broadly speaking, not small articles.
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are dealing here largely with large machines and indeed often machinery systems. In this situation I cannot imagine these people going very far in incurring substantial obligation without assuring themselves of where they stand with respect to the custom duties that are likely to be imposed.

That is exactly the point that I should like the minister to follow up. He is asking us to make what is in effect a new law with respect to custom-made goods, a law that has not existed previously. We should know how it is going to operate. Suppose there is no manufacturer for these custom-made goods. There may be a potential manufacturer but there is no actual manufacturer now. Every time someone comes to the Minister of National Revenue to make an inquiry about wanting to import some new kind of huge bulldozer from some other country, must the Minister of National Revenue refuse to answer what the duty on it will be until he searches from one end of Canada to the other in order to find out whether there is a potential manufacturer here and perhaps get by a construction season and put the work off to another year? That is the kind of practical problem that will arise in this case. As the minister so correctly stated, these are big machines or perhaps systems of machinery, where a big capital investment is going to take place,
Customs Tariff
and people are not going to want to wait six months while this question is being determined.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the hon. member may be unconsciously exaggerating the difficulty.
Perhaps so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We are not here in the realm in which there are great numbers of producers involved. There are perhaps not more than about eight or ten manufacturers of heavy machinery or large items of machinery in Canada. Hence the difficulty that the hon. member foresees in those proportions is not anticipated.
I made brief reference to the subject when I spoke on December 20 and drew attention to the fact that there is confidential information often available in these cases that enables the department to make rulings and to obtain what is required in the way of data from the producers who are concerned.
May I make just this one final observation. This matter is of interest not only with respect to the customs duties under the 70 particular items of the Customs Tariff to which I have referred but it is also of considerable importance in the administration of the anti-dumping laws. If hon. members will have regard to section 6, subsection 1 of the Customs Tariff they will see that dumping duties apply only in respect of goods of a class or kind made or produced in Canada. Accordingly all class or kind determinations are strictly relevant in this connection. The anti-dumping laws cannot be invoked unless what is concerned are goods of a class or kind made or produced in Canada.
In so far, therefore, as the new legislation results in "made" determinations in borderline cases, this will have the effect of enabling dumping to be dealt with by the application of the anti-dumping duty.

Mr. Chairman, at this stage of our debate we have an opportunity to elicit further information. It is true that the minister did describe his intentions in his budget speech of December 20 to an extent, but I was rather disappointed in some of the imponderables in connection with these proposals. We have had very little additional information given to us this afternoon beyond what was described when the minister spoke on this subject on December 20.
At this stage there are a number of questions that naturally arise because the minister's statement to date is lacking in the necessary information. The minister indicated that in an amendment of this type to the Customs Tariff Act the language that we find

Customs Tariff
in the resolution will compare very closely with the language that will appear at the next stage oi debate when we have before us the amending bill.
If that is so, and we accept that, I think all of us who have read the language in the resolution that is now before us will see very quickly that, far from finding here something in the nature of preciseness, in some of the essential factors we find the very opposite.
The hon. member for Welland raised a very pertinent question, which I have here in my notes and which arouses my curiosity in connection with the language of this resolution. It refers to the language and what is a "reasonable period of time".
Before we proceed from the resolution stage to discussion of the bill I think the minister should give us a much better explanation than he has so far provided as to what is a reasonable period of time. I felt that the explanation was very foggy indeed and it certainly did not satisfy the curiosity that I have as to the minister's intention in respect to a reasonable period of time.
Then I would draw the attention of the committee to another phrase which is certainly also very vague indeed. I think we must have some further explanation of the intention of the ministry in regard to it. I refer to the phrase in the very same section. What is going to be, in the opinion of the minister, "economic production"? That is indeed a very wide and broad phrase and would require considerable clarification.
While the minister recited perhaps six or seven times, simply as a statement, that there has been within the last decade, by reason of litigation, what he called an erosion of what was the original intent with respect to this item in the Customs Tariff, I was disappointed that he did not give any cases to illustrate what he had in mind in this respect. I think that as the debate continues we should hear from the minister a citation of some of the litigation and hearings before the tariff board and in the superior courts about which he complains and which he says are largely responsible for his decision to bring in this amending legislation.
I felt that the minister certainly skirted around section 3 of this proposed resolution when I think he used the phrase "The proposed legislation will give a broader discretion to the Minister of National Revenue in so far as decisions under this section are concerned". It is certainly not a matter of broader discretion. One simply has to read the language. It says here:
The decision of the minister shall be final with respect to-

This, that and the other thing. That certainly was the understatement of the day, when the minister attempted to brush aside this arbitrary power by saying that there is a broader discretion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member has unintentionally quite misunderstood my statement. I was drawing attention to the fact that the power of decision conferred on the minister applies in the one class of goods but not the other. I was dealing with the two classes of goods, one the custom-made class of goods and the other the shelf class of goods.

Mr. Chairman, one has only to read the language here, which is very plain:
The decision of the minister shall be final with respect to the following matters:
(a)	the normal Canadian consumption of the goods described in subsection (2), and
(b)	whether goods are custom-made to specifications, and whether adequate facilities exist in Canada for the economic production of such goods within a reasonable period of time.
When one reads that language one recognizes immediately that this is certainly not a matter of broader discretion, which was the mild description given by the minister, but the conferring upon the minister of arbitrary powers of very substantial consequence indeed, an absolute discretion in these matters which are matters of fact. I take it that the minister, with powers of this kind, could perhaps in his discretion make decisions that are contrary to fact, such as would be determined and have been determined hitherto by litigation by an appeal on the part of the taxpayer to our courts, our tariff board and the like.
That, with respect to these matters, is a right that is being taken away from the taxpayer. This, instead of providing preciseness and something definite, I suggest will actually bring in uncertainty on the part of the business community when they find that they are not going to be able to rely on a history of judicial decision. These matters are of utmost importance in their cost of production, because, as the minister said, most of these items of the custom-made type are exceedingly expensive and are perhaps a basic factor in the cost of production and in manufacturing of other goods that have to be produced in competition on a world wide basis.
I am satisfied that when these matters are not likely to be decided by rule of law and the recording of decisions of the tariff board and our courts, and depend, on the contrary, on the decision of a minister, many businessmen facing this uncertainty will perhaps

decide that they cannot go ahead with their plans because of the vagueness and uncertainties of this law.
I hope, Mr. Chairman, that we will hear from the minister further about some of the definitions of these broad phrases that are contained in the language of this resolution.
I refer to a reasonable period of time, economic production, adequate facilities and the like. speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
As the house is aware, the government has been giving active consideration to the situation of the oil industry in Canada for some time. It has had the benefit of a constructive report from the royal commission on energy, and the national energy board has studied intensively the changing conditions which have characterized the period since the commission reported.
I wish to inform the house that the government has decided upon a national oil policy which is, briefly, to achieve target levels of production of oil, including natural gas liquids, which will be set from time to time, and which will be designed to reach approximately 800,000 barrels a day in 1963. This objective for 1963 can be achieved by the industry on an economically sound basis, and will be approximately as high as the figure which would be achieved if the Montreal pipe line were to be constructed.
The production target level for the first part of this period will be an average of 640,000 barrels a day for the year 1961, with a level of not less than 625,000 barrels a day to be attained by mid-year. This compares with an average production of 550,000 barrels a day in 1960.
These targets are to be reached by increased use of Canadian oil in domestic markets west of the Ottawa valley, and by some expansion of export sales largely in existing markets which can be reached through established pipe lines.

National Oil Policy
The growth in domestic use is predicated in particular on substituting in Ontario markets west of the Ottawa valley products refined from Canadian crude for these now supplied from foreign crude. This will require in Ontario the displacement of the present small imports of crude, and a progressive reduction in imports of foreign products and transfers of products refined from foreign crudes in Montreal. Refining capacity in Ontario will have to be increased over the period so that by 1963 capacity is sufficient to enable the Ontario market west of the Ottawa valley to be supplied substantially from Canadian crudes.
The government program for expanded production of oil will be on a voluntary basis, but importers of crude and petroleum products will be required to report their imports monthly from January 1, 1961 in order to permit the national energy board to continue to assess the situation.
The increase in production of Canadian oil reflected in these target levels will of course require a sincere effort and full co-operation by all segments of the industry. The government desires that this effort and co-operation will be forthcoming without formal regulation.
The government has instructed the national energy board to evaluate the contribution of individual companies to the general efforts of the industry, as well as to report periodically on the progress of the program. If this progress suggests that voluntary efforts are not producing the results anticipated, then the government will take whatever further steps the circumstances may require to ensure the success of its policy, including the proclamation of section 87 of the National Energy Board Act, which provides for the regulation of imports and exports of oil.
In developing its policy the government has full regard to the interests of other countries which might be affected by its decisions. Its present program is designed to achieve the national objectives with the least possible disruption of normal trade patterns.
The increase in exports which is integral to the government's program is wholly consistent with the growth of sales of Canadian oil contemplated when exemption from United States oil import controls was established, under which Canadian oil is relatively free to move into the United States by overland means of transportation.
The progressive displacement of imported crudes and products in the Ontario market is considered to be fully consistent with the public announcement of the government of Venezuela that it considers that its oils should not reach these markets in the interior of Canada.
[Mr. Hees.l
The United States government has been made aware of the Canadian government's plans in view of the close connections between the oil economies of the two countries. Other interested governments are being informed today of the contents of the announcement which I have just made.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The house has listened with care and I am sure a great deal of interest to this statement which on the face of it appears to be an important statement emanating from the government with reference to the oil industry. After having looked at it carefully and at first blush this appears to us to be not a statement of national policy but only a repetition of what was contained in the recommendations of the Borden commission set up some few years ago.
As all hon. members know, the Borden commission presented to the governor in council in July of 1957 a special report on oil. The announcement today in our opinion is a faithful reproduction of the Borden commission's recommendations as they can be found at page 6-32 of the second report of the royal commission on energy. I should like to place on the record a brief summary of the recommendations of that commission:
To summarize, the commission recommends:
(1)	That it be national policy
(a)	to encourage and permit the export of Canadian crude oil without licence, and
(b)	to ensure the continued use, consistent with the interests of the Canadian consumer of petroleum products, of Canadian crude in refinery areas of Canada accessible to it by existing pipe line facilities, thereby increasing the market outlets for such crude oil.
(2)	That to implement such national policy the oil companies concerned take steps as soon as possible to displace, with products refined from Canadian crude, a volume of petroleum products now moving into the Ontario market from the Montreal refinery area equivalent to approximately 50,000 barrels daily of crude oil.
(3)	That to implement further such national policy the Canadian oil industry take vigorous and imaginative action very substantially to enlarge its markets in the United States on a basis that will ensure the continuing participation of Canadian crude in these markets and in their expansion.
(4)	That no government action should at this time be taken to ensure the construction of pipe line facilities to transport Canadian crude oil to the Montreal refinery area and that before any such action is taken an opportunity be given to the oil industry to demonstrate that it can find markets elsewhere in Canada and the United States sufficient to sustain a healthy and vigorous Canadian oil industry with the incentive for further exploration and development.
(5)	That, if government action should become necessary to implement the national policy we have recommended above, imports of crude oil be made subject to licence and that such licences be denied (except for some good and sufficient reason) to refiners in a refinery area in Canada where adequate pipe line facilities exist for the transportation of Canadian crude oil to meet the demands of such refinery area, but that crude oil

imported through a pipe line or by motor carrier or rail and produced in the country irom which such crude oil is imported be exempted from such licensing.
I ask the house to find the difference between the statement just made by the minister and the recommendations of the Borden commission which I have just read. I submit there is no difference in essence, between the two and I challenge the minister to point out any material difference between the recommendations I have just read and the statement he has made.
Of course, we will examine very carefully the statement that has been made and in due course and from time to time as the opportunity arises, we will make known our position on this policy. After listening to the statement, the only conclusion to be derived is that (1) it took the government two years to take cognizance of the report of the royal commission and (2) it took the government the two-year period preceding that to submit this matter to a royal commission on energy.

Mr. Speaker, the statement put before the house today by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) is undoubtedly an important one for a lagging Canadian oil industry. I believe that this announcement of policy by the government holds out the hope of renewed activity, renewed production and an increase in markets for our Canadian oil industry.
The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) appeared to be critical of the government's policy because he alleged it followed the royal commission's report. The report is in much greater detail than this statement. I know it follows it to some extent but I can see no reason to criticize the government for having gone forward with certain recommendations put before the country by this royal commission.
Business of the House
For many years hon. members of this group have advocated a national energy policy. We hope this is a step in the development of such a greatly needed national energy policy. I tell the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) that the type of policy enunciated today to deal with a difficult trade situation as far as the oil industry is concerned in the opinion of our group is a preferable one to that of increases in tariffs as a means of dealing with this problem.
We, of course, will have to study the target figures. We will concern ourselves with how this policy is implemented, with the allocation of markets among Canadian companies, and so on. We will have comments to make on this aspect of the policy as it unfolds.
It is well known to hon. members of this house that the international oil industry is in general an international cartel and to the extent that this policy will encourage production in Canada by independent oil companies we believe it will be a welcome policy in the opinion of Canadians. We like to see any government adopt the kind of social planning necessary to the welfare of ou! country.
